avertissement: Traductions automatiques des résumés et des titres français ; chaque nombre a été vérifié contre le français. Les documents de la Ville sont en français et font foi.

puces: The borough of Outremont is adopting a general by-law that allows its inspectors to visit properties to check that the regulations are being followed.
Officials responsible for enforcing the by-laws will be able to examine the inside and outside of land, houses and buildings at any reasonable hour.
Inspectors will have to identify themselves with a piece of identification if asked to do so.
Owners and occupants will have to let the inspector in, answer questions and not interfere with the inspector's work.
Anyone who breaks the by-law faces a fine of $1,000 to $4,000.
The by-law fills a gap: some Outremont by-laws, such as zoning (1177) and the PIIA (AO-530), did not provide for any power of inspection.
Adoption is planned for April 9, 2026, with a public notice of coming into force in April 2026; no existing by-law is repealed.

The borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles is authorizing the construction and occupancy of a "collective housing" building at 16330, rue Bureau, in the district of La Pointe-aux-Prairies.
The project may have a maximum of 110 rooms; no dwelling units or rooms in the basement.
Parking must be underground, with at least 42 spaces, plus 2 temporary spaces for people with reduced mobility near the drop-off area and at least 25 bicycle spaces.
The developer must keep or plant at least 20 trees, including 3 in front of the façade, preserve the mature trees and create a green roof on the canopy and the 2nd-floor terrace.
A free right-of-way easement will be registered with the City for an 8-metre-wide multi-purpose path.
Construction work must begin within 48 months; the landscaping must be completed within 24 months after the work starts.
A bank guarantee of $15,000 is required before the permits are issued; the City may keep it or have the work done if the deadlines are not met.
A similar project (PP-129) had been authorized in 2019, but the work was not done within the deadlines.
The City wants to close part of the lane located southwest of 89e Avenue, between rue Eugène-Couvrette and boulevard Perras, in Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles.
The land making up this lane would be transferred free of charge to the abutting owners, who already occupy it.
After the transfer, the City will collect property taxes on this land and will no longer have to manage the lane.
An easement is created on two lots to protect telecommunications and energy distribution installations.
The request comes from a citizen: 23 abutting owners said they were in favour, 3 were against and 3 did not respond.
One section of the lane remains City property because a steep drop in elevation makes it unusable for the abutting owners.
The city clerk will have to publish the notice of adoption in a daily newspaper and serve it on each abutting owner.

The borough of Le Plateau-Mont-Royal is amending, for a second time, its contract with the organization La bande musicale, which handles reception, supervision and management of the premises at the centre culturel Calixa-Lavallée.
The change concerns the schedule: the facility's opening hours are going to 48 hours per week.
The contract amount remains at a maximum of $48,000, including all applicable taxes, for the periods from August 26, 2024 to June 15, 2025 and from August 31, 2025 to June 14, 2026.
A first addendum, approved on June 2, 2025, had already adjusted the end dates, set the schedule at 69.5 hours per week and given priority to cultural activities for the rental of the premises.
The borough mayor (or the acting mayor) and the borough secretary are authorized to sign the documents.
The organization was selected following a call for projects held from November 17, 2023 to March 11, 2024, among three projects submitted.
The Mercier/Hochelaga-Maisonneuve borough council must decide whether to allow 15 units at 2735, avenue Bourbonnière, whereas the by-law allows 8 at most in this zone.
The request seeks to legalize work that was done: a 2016 permit provided for the reconfiguration of 8 units, but the building ended up with 16.
To comply with the rest of the regulations, one of the 16 units would have to be removed, hence the request for 15.
The building would have 14 studios of 333 to 367 sq. ft. and one 3½ unit of 619 sq. ft., whereas the 8 original units were 3½ units.

The Direction de l'aménagement urbain recommends refusal: risk of setting a precedent for non-compliant work, maintaining the planned density, and unfairness to neighbouring buildings that respected the limit of 8 units.
The comité consultatif d'urbanisme gave a unanimous unfavourable opinion on November 12, 2024.
Planned steps: public notice and posting on the building, then a decision by the borough council.
The City is amending its subsidy by-law for electrical service entrances related to burying wires on boulevard Gouin Ouest, between avenue Albert-Prévost and avenue Martin.
Seven addresses are being added to the list of subsidized properties: 12400 Albert-Prévost ($3,200) and 9041, 9043, 9055, 9095, 9185 and 9265 Gouin Ouest (from $4,100 to $13,700).
The subsidy for 9045, boulevard Gouin Ouest is increasing from $5,900 to $14,800.
Additional cost for the City: $79,100, taxes included, charged to the Programme d'élimination des poteaux.
The by-law aims to make the conversion of service connections happen at "no cost" for the affected owners.
Owners will be able to have their electrical service entrance modified after the work, once they have received the notice from the Commission des services électriques.

The City is officially notifying Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec (BAnQ) and the ministère de la Culture et des Communications that it wants to renegotiate their framework agreement, rather than let it renew automatically for five years starting January 1, 2027.
The Service de la culture, des sports et des loisirs and the Bureau des relations gouvernementales et municipales are mandated to carry out the negotiation.
This agreement sets out the City's annual contribution to BAnQ's operating expenses. BAnQ serves as the central library for Montrealers and as a resource for the local library network.
The current agreement, adopted in 2021, was extended to December 31, 2026. The authorized contribution was $13,997,461 per year in 2024 and 2025, then indexed to the CPI for 2026 with a cap of 2%.
The City justifies the renegotiation by the way the role of libraries has changed since 2002: digital services, new services and the expansion of the Montréal network.
Discussions have already been under way since January 2026; a new agreement is expected to be signed in 2027.
No impact on the 2026 financial framework.

City council appoints Andréanne Moreau, member of the executive committee responsible for culture, heritage, design and the French language, to the board of directors of the organization Les Arts et la Ville.
Her term is two years and is renewable; any earlier appointment becomes void.
She replaces Ericka Alneus, who sat on the board as an elected official representing the Ville.
The Ville has two reserved seats in this organization: one elected official and one staff member. Marie-Odile Melançon, division head at the Service de la culture, holds the staff seat.
No financial impact: board members serve on a volunteer basis.
According to the document, this network brings together Québec municipalities active in cultural development.
The urban agglomeration council is appointing Éric Duguay to the board of directors of the Conseil des arts de Montréal for three years; he replaces Agathe Alie.
He is scheduled to take office on January 29, 2026, the date of the urban agglomeration council.
Three current members — Josée Duplessis, Maxime Codère and Stanley Péan — have their terms renewed for a second three-year term.
The decision involves no spending: board members serve as volunteers.
The candidacies come from a governance and nominations committee, which reviews proposals from the cultural, business and education communities.
The City is renting hours on the indoor and outdoor running tracks at the complexe sportif Claude-Robillard (Ahuntsic-Cartierville) to Athlétisme Canada, plus a storage space of about 64 square feet.
The lease runs from February 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028 and provides for about 2,100 hours of use over three years.
The organization will pay rent estimated at $37,989, taxes included, billed each month based on actual use.
At the regular rate, the bill would be $109,947: the City is therefore granting a 67% discount (support of $71,958) and authorizing an additional budget for the same amount.
The facilities will be shared with the complex's regular activities, and the storage space with other organizations; no leasehold improvements are planned.
The agreement allows Montréal's national athletics centre to continue training athletes, even during the work at the complex.

The borough of Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce is renewing its contract with CMS Entrepreneurs Généraux for one year, to rent sidewalk-washing machines with operators, at a cost of $44,376.67 including taxes.
The contract covers the washing of 93.5 km of sidewalks (lot 3) in the spring of 2026, to remove the abrasives spread during the winter.
The work will start as soon as the temperature allows, in April-May 2026, and will last a maximum of 30 days.
The borough explains that it does not have enough equipment or staff to cover its whole territory itself.
This is the last extension allowed under the contract, which permitted two one-year renewals.
The expense, which is $40,521.82 after tax rebates, is paid out of the borough's public works operating budget.
The Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough is paying $80,000 (taxes included) to the Corporation de développement communautaire de Côte-des-Neiges for the year 2026, a second year in a row.
The money comes from the borough's unrestricted surplus.
The amount funds two joint-action efforts in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood: the Table habitation sociale and the Chantier salubrité.
The Chantier salubrité is to draw up a picture of unsanitary housing in the neighbourhood and share information about tenants' rights, prevention and health effects.
The Table habitation sociale is to support the development of social housing projects, a centralized list of applicants, workshops and the identification of potential sites.
The agreement starts in March 2026 and the organization must submit an annual report on January 30, 2027.
The decision summary cites data from 2021: 27.8% of households in the borough spend 30% or more of their income on housing, compared with 24.0% in Montréal.
The City accepts the donation of a white pine bonsai (Pinus strobus) offered by David Johnson to the Jardin botanique de Montréal.
It authorizes issuing a $3,700 tax receipt to the donor, a value set by an outside appraiser and including the "Tokoname" pot.
The tree, collected in 2002, is 36 inches tall and is believed to be between 35 and 45 years old; it was delivered to the Jardin botanique on August 18, 2024.
The specimen is being added to the Jardin botanique's bonsai collection and will be cared for by the institution's specialized horticulturist.
No communications activities are planned for this donation.
The borough of Le Sud-Ouest is granting a minor exemption for the bibliothèque Eva-Circé-Côté, at 1050, rue d'Hibernia.
The library will be allowed to provide 11 indoor bicycle parking spaces, instead of the 17 required by the planning by-law.
The request is tied to the library's expansion permit: 2,320 m² is being added, for a total area of 3,380 m².
According to the file, other bike racks will be installed outside during the redevelopment of the adjacent public space.
The borough argues that adding the 6 missing spaces indoors would require major changes to the plans and would delay the project.
The comité consultatif d'urbanisme gave a favourable opinion on December 9, 2025; a public notice will precede the adoption of the resolution.
The borough of Le Sud-Ouest is renewing the terms of two regular members of its planning advisory committee (comité consultatif d'urbanisme, or CCU): Émilie Julien and Patrick Ouellet.
Their term lasts two years, from February 10, 2026 to February 10, 2028.

The CCU reviews behind closed doors the proposed changes to the Plan d'urbanisme and to the planning by-laws, minor exemptions, specific projects, applications covered by the Règlement sur les PIIA and conditional uses, and then makes recommendations to the borough council.
The same members make up the committee that reviews demolition applications, which sits in public and issues decisions, with a right of appeal to the borough council.
The renewal is meant to keep the meetings and recommendations going; no cost is indicated.
The resolution is to be adopted by the borough council on February 9, 2026.
Hydro-Québec wants to build a new electrical transformer substation (315-25 kV) at the corner of boulevard de l'Assomption and rue Hochelaga, in Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve.

Two underground power lines of about 5 km each will connect the poste Notre-Dame to the new poste Hochelaga, running notably along rue Notre-Dame Est, rue Beauclerk, rue La Fontaine, rue Ontario Est, rue de Marseille and avenue Haig.
The new substation is meant to relieve the poste Longue-Pointe and poste Jeanne-d'Arc and to support the residential, commercial and industrial development planned in the area.
The agglomeration declares the project consistent with the objectives of its land use planning and development plan; this is not an approval of the project itself.
About one quarter of the substation site (one hectare) will be planted with vegetation, with an open-air stormwater retention basin.
The lines cross an area of archaeological interest: surveys have been carried out and monitoring is planned during excavation work, with work stopping if anything is found.
Hydro-Québec estimates the investment at $444M, with work expected to begin in 2026 and service starting in 2029.
The City confirms that Hydro-Québec's project meets the objectives of the Schéma d'aménagement de l'agglomération de Montréal.
Hydro-Québec wants to build a new 315-kilovolt underground power line, 2.2 km long, between the postes des Irlandais and Guy, in Le Sud-Ouest and Ville-Marie.
The routes being considered run along rue Bridge, then rue Saint-Patrick, and go north along rue Guy or rue Richmond.
This line replaces line L3043 as part of the replacement of poste Guy, which supplies a dense downtown area and is having equipment problems.
Hydro-Québec estimates the investment at about $26M, with work planned to start in spring 2026 and service beginning in fall 2027.
The route crosses an area of archaeological interest; a potential study and archaeological inventories have been carried out.
The City's opinion deals only with compliance with the Schéma and is not an approval of the project.
The City is entering into a 36-month agreement with APTQ inc. to supply RFID tags for the books, printed materials and discs of the réseau des bibliothèques de Montréal.
Estimated amount of the agreement: $256,543.72, taxes included, from January 7, 2026 to January 6, 2029.
Expected quantities: 780,000 white tags at $0.21, 90,000 translucent tags at $0.22 and 67,000 disc films at $0.59.
APTQ inc. is the lowest compliant bidder out of three bids received; one bid was rejected because it lacked a bid guarantee.
The estimate takes into account purchases from 2022 to 2024 and the tagging of the collection of the new library at the Centre Sanaaq.
The City did not extend the previous agreement with Bibliotheca Canada inc., since the planned indexing brought no actual price adjustment.
APTQ inc.'s performance will be evaluated as part of the contract.
The urban agglomeration council is changing the 2026 towing rates by modifying the vehicle weight categories: the limit goes from 4,500 kg to 3,000 kg.
The three categories therefore go back to being: under 3,000 kg, from 3,000 to 8,000 kg, and 8,000 kg and over.
These categories are what determine which towing rate applies to a vehicle within the territory of the Ville de Montréal.
The SPVM wants to avoid having two different rate scales in 2026: the one in the by-law and the one in towing contract 23-19687, which was extended by one year.
Beyond 10 km of towing, vehicles of 3,000 kg or less pay $4.00 per additional kilometre.
The return to the ministère des Transports categories is planned for July 1, 2027, along with the next towing contract.
The City says the change has no impact on its finances, since these rates are paid by residents to the towing companies.
The urban agglomeration council must appoint Julien Hénault-Ratelle, the councillor for the Tétreaultville district, to the board of directors of PME MTL Centre-Est.
The Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve borough council chose him unanimously on December 17, 2025, at a special meeting.
The general by-laws of PME MTL Centre-Est require the borough to name one of its elected officials to sit on the board of directors, subject to approval by the urban agglomeration.
PME MTL Centre-Est is a local economic development organization that supports entrepreneurs.
The file involves no spending: no financial aspect is planned.
The borough of Montréal-Nord is adding $20,818.75 (taxes included) to the contract for disposing of street-sweeping residue, bringing the total to $147,101.54.
The contract is awarded to Recyclage Notre-Dame inc., whose site is located at 11400, avenue Racette, in Montréal-Nord.
The additional amount covers 226.68 more metric tonnes than the 1,375 tonnes planned, for a total of 1,601.68 tonnes until December 31, 2025.
The prices paid are $45.88 per tonne for disposal and $34.00 per tonne in fees, plus taxes.
The residue (fine sand, stone dust, dead leaves, paper and plastic) is transported by the borough's blue-collar workers, then weighed on site.
The expense is paid out of the operating budget of the Direction des travaux publics.
The contract comes from a City-wide framework agreement valid from January 31, 2023 to January 30, 2027.
The City is lending archaeological objects and human bones from its Réserve des collections archéologiques to the Site historique Marguerite-Bourgeoys, in Vieux-Montréal.
These artifacts will be used in the temporary exhibition "BjFj-196 : les secrets de Bonsecours," which marks 30 years of archaeological digs at the site.
The exhibition is set to open on June 17, 2026; the objects are scheduled to be transported on April 13, 2026.
The loan is planned for a period of three years, and the objects may only be used for exhibition purposes.
The agreement sets out the conditions for conserving, managing and showcasing the objects; the list of the items being lent is attached as an appendix.
The City says the agreement involves no additional cost: storage and management fees are paid out of the Réserve's own budget.

In April 2026, the City is submitting an application for the Cap-Saint-Jacques area (Grand parc de l'Ouest, 330 hectares) to obtain DarkSky International's "Urban Night Sky Place" international designation.

To obtain the designation, the City commits to producing a lighting management plan, bringing all light fixtures in the area up to standard, setting rules for light brought in by visitors, and guaranteeing public access at night.
The project includes facilities for stargazing, educational programming on astronomy and nighttime biodiversity, and measures to protect ecological corridors.

No financial commitment is required to submit the application. If the designation is granted, estimated costs include $250,000 to bring the lighting up to standard (2026-2036), $90,000 for the facilities and signs, $40,000 for activity content, plus about $34,500 a year in recurring costs.
Timeline: DarkSky's answer is expected in April 2027, the lighting plan is to be submitted in February 2027, and the site is to be fully compliant in April 2032.
The file is led by the Service des grands parcs, du Mont-Royal et des sports together with the Service de l'Espace pour la vie; the decision rests with the urban agglomeration council.
The document mentions only one other designated site in Canada, parc du Mont-Bellevue in Sherbrooke (2022), out of thirteen worldwide.
The borough of Le Plateau-Mont-Royal is adding $21,475 to the YMCA du Parc for its "Intervention jeunesse au chalet Baldwin" project.
This amount is added to the $26,464 already granted in December 2025, which allows the project to be extended into fall 2026.
The project aims at prevention work with young people from école secondaire Jeanne-Mance and at how people share the space in parc Baldwin, in particular vandalism.
The borough is relying on the 2025 accountability report, which shows positive results.
The agreement is amended to add two payments, an updated follow-up sheet and an additional budget; the organization has signed the addendum.
The expense is paid entirely by the central city, through the budget of the Prévention Montréal program.
The urban agglomeration council must approve the 2026 budget of the Société du parc Jean-Drapeau, the non-profit organization that manages the park.
The 2026 budget plans for $40,080.4K in revenue and $40,763.6K in spending, a deficit of $683.1K covered by a reserve allocation of the same amount.
The City will pay $15.6M to the Société in 2026, after $15.3M in 2025.
Staffing goes from 319.4 to 340.9 person-years, an increase of 21.5.
For 2025, the Société expects a deficit of $1.186M offset by $1.262M in reserves, for a surplus of $76K.

The document also presents the 2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Works Program and the 2025 achievements: Rive-Sud access, reopening of the tour de Lévis, Place des Nations, conversion of parking lots into green spaces.
The filing takes place at the January 12, 2026 meeting and approval is planned for January 29, 2026.
The urban agglomeration council must approve the 2026 budget of the Corporation d'habitation Jeanne-Mance, which manages 788 units for low-income households in the Quartier Latin, downtown.
The total budget comes to $25,242,739 for 2026, compared with $23,563,293 in 2025.

Replacement, improvement and modernization (RAM) work accounts for $17,213,854, including stormwater retention, bringing the towers up to fire safety standards, and drainage and firebreak fixes at the tower at 250, rue Ontario.
The total deficit of $20,232,375 is covered 75% by the CMHC and 25% by the Ville de Montréal, whose share is paid by the Communauté métropolitaine de Montréal.
Revenues rise to $5,010,364, an increase of 22% attributed to the fact that 85% of the modernized units are now rented.
Maintenance and janitorial expenses are up 10%, mainly because of the elevators and of security related to downtown social issues.
The tabling is scheduled for the January 12, 2026 meeting and the approval for the January 29, 2026 meeting.
The urban agglomeration council must approve the 2026 budget of the Office municipal d'habitation de Montréal (OMHM): tabled on January 12, 2026, with approval expected on January 29, 2026.
The OMHM's total budget goes from $541M in 2025 to $605.6M in 2026, including $475.4M for low-rental housing (HLM) and $81M for rent supplements.
The OMHM plans $250M in major work and the rollout of a 20-year asset maintenance plan for all of its housing stock.
The organization will open four local service points and set up a single telephone line for tenants and applicants.
The OMHM houses 42,587 households, with 20,810 HLM units (about 11,000 of them for people 60 and over) and 18,572 rent supplement units.
In 2026, the federal funding agreement will have expired for 63% of HLM buildings; Québec and the Communauté métropolitaine de Montréal continue to cover the operating deficit.
The OMHM expects to pay $33.8M in municipal and school taxes and to roll out its Plan climat across its real estate holdings.
The urban agglomeration council must approve the 2026 budget of the Conseil des arts de Montréal, tabled on January 12, 2026 for a vote on January 29, 2026.
The City announced at the end of December that its contribution to the organization will increase by $2.5M in 2026, after a budget freeze in 2025 (a first since 2007).
This increase will be used to raise the budgets of programs that were cut in recent years and to top up the grants of about 335 arts organizations that receive mission-based funding.
In 2025, the Conseil des arts planned to invest $20,066,080 in support for artists, organizations and collectives, which is 91% of the agglomeration's contribution.
The four-year program pays out $11M a year to 336 organizations, a commitment of $44M from 2024 to 2027.
In November 2025, the Tribunal administratif du travail certified the Syndicat canadien de la fonction publique to represent the employees of the Conseil des arts.
Staffing went from 21.22 full-time employees in 2016 to 37 in 2024, then to 35 in 2025 after two positions were lost through attrition.
City council must approve the 2026 budget of the Agence de mobilité durable, which manages paid parking in Montréal.
The budget is tabled at the special meeting of January 12, 2026 and will be submitted for approval on January 28, 2026.
For 2025, the Agence expects revenues of $80.2M (instead of the $83M budgeted), mainly because of a $3.2M drop in management revenues.
Its 2025 expenses have also been revised downward, to $82.2M, with $2.5M more devoted to monitoring, especially during the snow removal period.

The number of paid on-street spaces reached 18,422 as of June 30, 2025, which is 926 more than a year earlier, with additions in Le Plateau-Mont-Royal, Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie, Le Sud-Ouest, Verdun and Ville-Marie.
Some spaces were removed to set up bus stops and to clear 5 m at intersections.
For 2026-2028, the Agence is planning new mobility hubs, a mobility data portal, a curbside inventory and the management of off-street parking.
The 2026 budget provides for 687.9 person-years at the Agence.

The borough of Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie is amending three of its by-laws (zoning by-law 01-279, specific projects by-law RCA-148 and demolition by-law RCA-6) to bring them in line with the Plan d'urbanisme et de mobilité 2050 adopted by the City in June 2025.
More than one hundred sections and appendices are being revised, in particular to remove provisions that have become incompatible with the new plan.

Housing for people in unstable housing situations becomes permitted everywhere in the borough, except in zones limited to 8 dwellings or fewer, where the conditional uses procedure will have to be followed.
A service facility for these same people is permitted at 5800, rue Saint-Denis; elsewhere, approval through conditional uses will be required.

Maintenance facilities for wheeled public transit (buses, paratransit) are permitted at Espace Affaires Rosemont, at the Cour de service des Carrières and at the Technopôle Angus; those for rail transit (metro, REM, tramway) are permitted everywhere.
New commercial uses are being regulated: mobility hubs (between Boyer and Saint-André, and behind the Promenade Masson), micro urban distribution centres and pickup counters.

The borough is adding assessment criteria for work on institutional and industrial heritage complexes and in visual corridors; a public consultation was held on February 26, 2026, and the STM submitted a written opinion.
The Government of Québec is giving the City two more years, until October 31, 2027, to sell a first piece of land on the site of the former hippodrome.
The land is located west of boulevard Décarie and south of rue Paré, in Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, and is part of the future écoquartier Namur-Hippodrome.
The previous deadline, set for October 31, 2025, has already passed; the City had asked for the extension on October 10, 2025.
The City had acquired this 434,756.8-square-metre site in 2017 from SONACC and the Government of Québec, with no immediate payment.
The extension does not involve any financial compensation, and the other conditions of the transfer deed remain the same.
The City points to the planning steps still to be done, carried out in particular with GALOPH, a group created in 2023 with the two levels of government and housing stakeholders.
The City is awarding 4 contracts to inject TreeAzin insecticide into ash trees, from June 22 to August 28, 2026, for a total expense of $724,537.53 including taxes.
EspacesVerts is getting lot 1 ($136,312.64) and Bio-Contrôle Arboricole inc. lots 2, 3 and 4 ($443,317.39).
On top of that, there is $57,963 in contingencies and $86,944.50 for variations in quantities; the central city covers the entire expense.
About 16,400 public ash trees and 3,150 private ash trees are to be treated in 2026, compared with the 12,000 and 2,000 planned for 2025.

The three public lots cover specific boroughs (including Lachine, LaSalle, Ville-Marie, Anjou, Montréal-Nord, Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Pierrefonds-Roxboro); lot 4 covers private ash trees in all 19 boroughs.
Public call for tenders 25-21239 drew 3 bids out of 5 people who took out the tender documents; the prices selected are 9.7% to 54.2% below the City's estimates.
The City is awarding AFI par Edgenda inc. three contracts (lots 1, 2 and 3) to design and produce online training for its staff.
The agreements are worth $1,059,350.90, taxes included: $454,007.53 for lot 1, $454,007.53 for lot 2 and $151,335.84 for lot 3.
The agreements last 2 years, with 2 options to extend by one year each.
The City will pay only for the services actually requested; the costs will be charged to the budgets of the boroughs, the central departments and the related cities.
Public call for tenders 25-21139 received 10 bids, 4 of which were found compliant; AFI par Edgenda obtained the best final score.
The selected price is 37.05% below the City's estimate for lots 1 and 2; the firm says this is based on competitive pricing and economies of scale.
The City will carry out a performance evaluation of the firm.
The borough of Le Plateau-Mont-Royal agrees to have the borough of Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie handle the maintenance of lighting, signage and road markings on its territory in 2026.
Cost for Le Plateau-Mont-Royal: $2,709,400.

This centralized service has existed since 2004 and covers the nine boroughs of the former Ville de Montréal, including Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce, Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, Ville-Marie and Le Sud-Ouest.
The Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie borough council made this service offer on November 27, 2025.
If it had refused, the borough would have had to hire outside suppliers to do this work.
The Verdun borough is giving out $200 in bursaries for the Journées de la persévérance scolaire 2026.
Two bursaries of $100 will be drawn at random among the participants.
The presentation takes place on Tuesday, February 17, 2026, from 1:30 p.m. to 4 p.m., at the borough hall.
The event is organized with the Table de concertation jeunesse de Verdun and highlights the journey of adult learners of all ages with a certificate of recognition.
The amount is included in the borough's 2026 budget; the same amount has been granted every year since 2019.
The City is giving $10,000 to Les Amis du Jardin botanique de Montréal for bird-themed guided tours at the Jardin botanique in 2026.
The money will be used to train volunteer guides, buy observation equipment and produce educational materials.
The payment will be made in two parts: $9,000 within 30 days after the agreement is signed, then $1,000 after the activity report is submitted, no later than January 31, 2027.
The money comes from a donation from the Fondation Espace pour la vie received in September 2025 and is paid 100% by the central city.
The agreement with the organization ends on December 31, 2026.
The project is part of the « Un jardin pour les oiseaux » program, which focuses on educational activities and citizen science.
The City is awarding a direct-negotiation contract to Anne Lagacé to design and install the multimedia features of the 2026 edition of Jardins de Lumière, at the Jardin botanique.
The total expense comes to $574,696.79, taxes included (net amount of $499,845, with a 100% tax rebate), paid in 5 instalments in 2026 and covered entirely by the central city.
The contract covers the design, set-up, take-down and technical follow-up of the light exhibition "Résonances", which is scheduled to open on August 28, 2026.
The route renews the portion located in the Jardin des Premières-Nations, which has been lit according to the same concept since 2021; it includes five immersive scenes.
The design team brings together Indigenous people (Marie-Andrée Gill, Soleil Launière, Euroma Awashish) and non-Indigenous people (Anne Lagacé, Gonzalo Soldi).
The proposal was selected following a call for proposals; the Jardin botanique is to receive $80,000 from the Fondation Espace pour la vie for this project.
According to the document, the event draws about 150,000 visitors a year in September and October.

The City is awarding Pronex Excavation inc. a contract worth $21,906,593.97 (taxes included), the lowest of the 11 bids received; with contingencies ($2,623,942.57) and incidentals ($4,390,496.71), the total spending comes to $28,921,033.25.

The work covers rue Guy between Saint-Jacques and René-Lévesque Ouest (rebuilding water mains and a complete redesign of the street), rue Guy between William and Saint-Jacques (surface work) and rue Saint-Jacques between des Seigneurs and Guy (pipe rehabilitation), in the boroughs of Le Sud-Ouest and Ville-Marie.

Planned work includes: new 500 and 600 mm main water pipes over 465 m, a secondary pipe enlarged from 200 to 300 mm over 490 m, replacement of service connections including two made of lead, sewers at the Saint-Antoine intersection, a gas pipe, sidewalks and granite curbs, raised bike paths, green drainage infrastructure, traffic lights and lighting, and archaeological digs.

Steel and virtual clearance frames will be installed on each side of the CPKC railway bridge to protect the structure from truck collisions (about 50 per year); a maintenance agreement with CPKC has yet to be finalized.
The pipes in question date from 1890 to 1912, and four breaks have been recorded on this section over six years.
The construction site is planned from the second quarter of 2026 to December 2027; the contractor will pay 0.1% of the contract price for each day of delay, with a minimum of $1,000 per day.
The bill is shared between the agglomeration (53.10%), the central city (22.70%) and the Commission des services électriques de Montréal (24.20%); the contractor's performance will be evaluated.
The Outremont borough is awarding the cleaning of its municipal buildings to UNIVAP inc. for $583,595.85, taxes included.
The contract runs from March 1, 2026 to February 28, 2029, with two renewal options of one year each.

Five buildings are covered: the borough hall (543, ch. de la Côte-Sainte-Catherine), the council chamber (530, av. Davaar), the bibliothèque Robert-Bourassa and the Galerie d'art (41, av. Saint-Just), the service yard (600, av. de la Gare-de-Triage) and 1431, av. Van Horne.
The company must supply its own equipment and use products that meet the borough's requirements.
UNIVAP is the lowest compliant bidder: its price is 36% below the estimate of $907,849.50; the current contractor ranked 7th at $832,698.96.
Of the 18 bids submitted, 6 were found to be non-compliant.
The expense is paid entirely by the borough, out of its operating budget.
The City is hiring the non-profit organization Nature-Action Québec inc. to manually pull out and cut invasive exotic plants in the large parks, for $1,602,751 (taxes not applicable).
With contingencies ($80,137.55) and incidental costs ($48,082.53), the total spending comes to $1,730,971.08.
The contract runs from March 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028, with an annual report in December 2026, 2027 and 2028.
The work includes manual and motorized cutting, pulling out plants, geomatic tracking of the treated areas and disposal of plant waste, under the supervision of the City's biologists.
The contract is awarded without a call for tenders, an exception allowed by law for contracts made with a non-profit organization.
The submitted price is 0.67% higher than the in-house estimate made in October 2025.
The spending is paid by the urban agglomeration, because it concerns the parcs-nature, and funded by a loan by-law tied to the Plan de gestion de la forêt urbaine.
The borough of Saint-Léonard is giving $461,200 to five organizations for youth activities in 2025-2026, as part of the project "Animation, jeunesse, actions à Saint-Léonard".
The money comes from the ministère de la Sécurité publique, which signed a $472,200 agreement with the borough on February 26, 2026.

The two largest amounts go to Centre Horizon Carrière ($212,700) for a coordination team and activities at the Centre communautaire Leonardo da Vinci, and to Centre communautaire Leonardo da Vinci ($206,000) to pay rent and make its premises accessible to youth organizations.
Club basketball St-Léonard is receiving $14,000 to run activities in the teen zone of the pavillon Giuseppe-Garibaldi and on the park's outdoor courts.
La Maison de jeunes de Saint-Léonard is receiving $13,000 to run activities at the skatepark in parc Delorme and $3,500 for a youth-led snow brigade helping seniors.
Le Collectif jeunesse de Saint-Léonard is receiving $12,000 for an awareness campaign on the feeling of safety ("Rues citoyennes - volet 2 2.0").
The borough says its goals are to reduce violence among young people and increase the feeling of safety, following several incidents since 2021.

The borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles adopts the second drafts of two resolutions concerning two lots on boulevard Métropolitain Est (12345 and 12525), and takes note of the minutes of the public consultations held on November 25, 2025.

At 12345, boulevard Métropolitain Est, the expansion of a commercial building is authorized despite the zoning rules (use classes, front setback, masonry, parking access, parking in the front yard, ground sign).

Conditions at 12345: a ground sign no more than 9.5 m, parking access no more than 15 m, display limited to 8 cars in a specific area, at least 20 bicycle racks, planting of at least 44 trees plus a wooded area in the back yard monitored annually.
Other requirements: permeable ground coverings in front of the expansion and near the façade, screens to hide mechanical equipment, and a landscaping plan signed by a landscape architect.
The developer must provide three irrevocable bank guarantees: $50,000 for the expansion and greening, $100,000 for the wooded area at the back and $25,000 for the subdivision.

At 12525, boulevard Métropolitain Est, the rules of project PP-86 are amended: parking access no more than 15 m, a sign no more than 8 m, and removal of the billboard on lot 1 866 166 before the new car dealership opens.

Work must begin within 24 months after the resolutions come into force, otherwise the authorization becomes void; the landscaping work has separate deadlines (12 months at 12525, 6 months after construction at 12345).
The borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles is approving the plans to convert the commercial building at 11901 to 11905, rue Notre-Dame Est, in Vieux Pointe-aux-Trembles.
The upper floors will become residential: 7 units in all, namely 2 on the 2nd and 3rd floors and 3 on the 4th floor. This change of use was authorized on April 1, 2025.
Three new fixed windows in brown aluminum (1.21 m x 1.7 m) will be added at the back, one per floor, in the shared corridor.

The sheet metal entablatures, which are in poor condition, will be removed and replaced in order to preserve the original appearance; the electrical wiring above the storefront windows will be removed.
The small paved area on the 8e Avenue side will be landscaped with perennials and other plantings.
The urban planning advisory committee, which was unanimously in favour on April 10, 2026, is asking that the quantity of perennials be reduced and that low-spreading perennials or grasses be used.
The borough of Lachine is approving changes to the façades of buildings B, C and B+ of the former Maison mère des Sœurs de Sainte-Anne, at 1950, rue Provost.

The changes requested on December 9, 2025 affect, among other things, the windows, the glass doors, a lower canopy, the replacement of the damaged terracotta cladding on wing C, and the screens hiding the rooftop equipment.
The permit is granted on the condition that the entire project complies with the regulations in force; any new modification will have to go through site planning approval (PIIA) again.
The site is in a heritage area, which makes approval mandatory for changes to architectural features.
According to the Direction de l'aménagement urbain, the work is necessary and does not result in any major change to the project already approved.
This work is part of phase 2 of the convent's conversion: redevelopment of wings B and C and the addition of the 8-storey B+ extension, for 270 housing units and 124 parking spaces.
The City is renewing the lease of a vacant lot to the Société de transport de Montréal (STM), south of rue Louvain and west of boulevard Saint-Laurent, in Ahuntsic-Cartierville.
The 2,787 m² (30,000 sq. ft.) lot is used as free parking reserved for STM employees' vehicles displaying a permit sticker.
The lease runs for three years starting October 1, 2026, but only 92 days a year, from October 1 to December 31.
The STM will pay the City $49,293 in total: $15,947 in 2026, $16,426 in 2027 and $16,920 in 2028, before taxes.
The STM pays the operating costs and property taxes, if any; the City does not have to maintain this part of the lot.
Either of the two parties may end the lease with 60 days' written notice.
STM employees use this parking lot to check their list of routes from time to time, a list that should eventually be computerized.
The City is extending the lease of a city-owned lot to the company 9413-8757 Québec inc. (Clicknpark) by 2 years and 4 months, from September 1, 2026 to December 31, 2028.
The 836 m² (9,000 sq. ft.) lot is located in Ahuntsic-Cartierville, south of rue Louvain Ouest and west of boulevard Saint-Laurent.
It is used as a paid parking lot reserved for members who use the Clicknpark app, in the District central.
The City will collect total rent of $45,049 before taxes, or $2.11/sq. ft. ($18,981 for the first year).
The tenant pays the operating costs and property taxes, if any; the City does not maintain the lot.
Either party may end the lease with 60 days' written notice.
The City has been leasing this lot to Clicknpark since 2023, following a pilot project on parking sharing.
The City wants to borrow $10,538,000 to build a public park on the classified archaeological site of Fort-Lorette, in Ahuntsic-Cartierville, which the City bought in 2018 for $5,691,262.50.
The money will cover professional services, soil decontamination if needed, burying the electrical wires, a temporary shoreline path and the park's landscaping.
The project is meant to improve the pedestrian link between parc-nature de l'Île-de-la-Visitation and boulevard Gouin Est, with a walkway along the shoreline strip.

Planned schedule: burying the power line and the temporary path in fall 2026, plans and specifications in 2028, park work in 2029-2030, depending on how Hydro-Québec's work on the shoreline progresses.
Spending on the existing building on the site is not covered: the City has not yet decided whether it will be converted or demolished.
On May 7, 2025, the City committed to reimbursing Hydro-Québec up to $100,000 in engineering costs if the project is dropped before the implementation agreement.
The loan will be repaid over a maximum of 20 years; upkeep of the future facilities will be the responsibility of the borough of Ahuntsic-Cartierville.
The City is launching a public competition to choose a work of art that will be integrated into the Bibliothèque Saint-Charles (Éva-Circé-Côté), in Le Sud-Ouest.
It is authorizing spending of $34,492.50 (taxes included) to hold the competition and cover the project's general expenses.

The competition is open to professional Québec artists; the work will be a bas-relief hung from the soffits of the cantilevered roof, with an optional secondary intervention on a column and two façades.

Artists will have to draw inspiration from values linked to Éva Circé-Côté or to the Pointe-Saint-Charles neighbourhood: civic engagement, social struggles, inclusion, democratization of knowledge, and freedom of thought.
A jury of seven people (visual arts specialists, an architect, the borough, a citizens' representative, and the Service de la culture) will select up to four finalists, then a winner.

Planned timeline: launch in January 2026, submission of applications on February 20, 2026, selection of the winner in September 2026, contract in November 2026, and installation of the work in April 2028.
The total cost of the public art project is estimated at $348,041.33, taxes included; the purchase of the work will be the subject of a separate decision.

The City has reached an agreement with artist Jonathan Villeneuve to remove the electronic components of the artwork "Lux Obscura," installed on rue Émery in the Quartier des spectacles since April 2018.
Only the steles and the glass panels will be kept, and they will be used to present temporary or permanent art exhibitions.

Reasons given: the lack of a fibre optic network and the winter make maintenance difficult and costly, the artwork has not been working for a few years, and it has been repeatedly hit by graffiti and had a glass panel broken in 2020.
No compensation is being paid to the artist for this change.
Announced timeline: adoption of the addendum in January 2026, modification of the artwork and addition of artistic content in March 2026, then promotion of the works on display.
The original contract, awarded in October 2016, provided $218,452.50 for the fabrication and installation of the artwork, within a total expenditure of $252,945.
The City is entering into an 18-month master agreement with Groupe ABS inc. to analyze soil contamination, up to a maximum of $813,313.60, taxes included.
These analyses are used to determine the nature and degree of contamination of soil excavated during underground conduit work sites, so that it can be disposed of according to the standards in force.
The services would begin in March 2026 and end after 18 months or as soon as the maximum amount is reached.
Groupe ABS inc. received the best score among the 3 bids received (11 firms had obtained the tender documents) in public call for tenders S-2345.
The selected price is $244,263.82 (23%) lower than the City's most recent internal estimate.
The expense is fully covered by the Commission des services électriques de Montréal and reimbursed through fees paid by its users.
The firm's performance will be evaluated.
The City is entrusting the STM with carrying out its own municipal work at the future Pie-IX and Viau stations, on rue Jean-Talon Est, and will pay it up to $3,808,451.29, taxes included.
The STM will act as project manager: it will issue the calls for tenders, supervise the work and assign it to the contractor building the two stations.

The City undertakes to provide the plans, specifications and estimates, to give technical assistance and to reimburse the STM for the actual costs as well as its share of the supervision, quality control and traffic management costs.
The goal is to carry out the City's work at the same time as the metro work, to reduce costs and shorten traffic disruptions.
The blue line extension adds five stations over about 6 km, from Saint-Michel to Anjou; the stations are scheduled to open in 2031.
Schedule: signing of the agreement in March 2026, awarding of the contracts in August and October 2026, metro work from 2026 to 2030 and the City's work integrated in 2028-2029.

The expense will be paid 95% by the central city and 5% by the agglomeration; the redevelopment of rue Jean-Talon Est covers 3.5 km, from 22e avenue to the first traffic light east of boulevard Langelier.
The borough of Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension is amending its by-law on specific projects (PPCMOI) to bring it into line with the Plan d'urbanisme et de mobilité 2050.

The by-law adds definitions: building of heritage interest, institutional heritage complex, place of worship and associated building, area of archaeological interest, visual corridor, accessory dwelling unit, among others.
A "major project" is defined by specific thresholds: removal of more than 20% of the above-ground volume, construction of more than 50 m², addition of a parking area with more than six spaces, etc.

Developers will have to submit new documents: a waste management plan covering the three streams (recycling, organic matter, garbage), and traffic impact studies for the redevelopment of a large pericentral commercial complex.

After a review by the Service d'urbanisme et de mobilité, the borough is adding heritage conservation criteria: the demolition of an essential element will have to be justified by a danger, an unsalvageable condition or the technical impossibility of repairing it.
The file also includes the minutes of the public consultation meeting of March 18, 2026 and the report on the written consultation held from March 11 to 18, 2026.

The City is accepting a grant from the ministère des Affaires municipales et de l'Habitation to build a permanent flood protection structure within the rue Crevier right-of-way, in Ahuntsic-Cartierville.
The structure, about 275 metres long, will be located between boulevard Gouin and the rivière des Prairies.
Total project cost: $2,974,000. Québec is contributing $2,265,806 (75% plus an amount for the QST) and the borough is paying $708,194.
Work began on August 18, 2025 with the installation of sheet piles; the concrete facing panels are planned for 2026 and the work is to be completed by March 31, 2027.
The borough's director of territorial development is authorized to sign the agreement and related documents.
Reason given: the floods of 2017, 2019 and 2023 caused damage and required costly temporary measures (more than $135,000 in human resources in 2023, with 94 people mobilized over two months).

The urban agglomeration council is being asked to appoint Maude Théroux-Séguin, mayor of Ahuntsic-Cartierville, as the borough's representative on the board of directors and the executive committee of PME-MTL Centre-Ouest, starting in January 2026.
PME-MTL Centre-Ouest serves Côte-Saint-Luc, Hampstead, Montréal-Ouest, Mont-Royal, as well as the boroughs of Ahuntsic-Cartierville and Saint-Laurent.

Its board of directors has 14 people: 4 elected officials and 10 people from the business community, including the chair. Ahuntsic-Cartierville has one elected official and 4 business people on it; the latter do not have to be appointed by the agglomeration.

According to the document, having an elected official present is meant to ensure consistency and follow-up on the joint actions of the organization and the borough, and ensures continuity in the support and funding of business projects for companies in the area.
There is no financial aspect attached to this file.
The borough council adopted the recommendation unanimously on November 26, 2025; PME-MTL Centre-Ouest will announce the final makeup of its board after its next meeting.

The borough of LaSalle is giving $40,000 to the Centre culturel et communautaire Henri-Lemieux (CCCHL) for its program "Favorisons nos échanges avec les communautés ethnoculturelles laSalloises" in 2026.
The program promotes the arts and culture of diverse communities, creates opportunities for intercultural exchange, and introduces people to the cultural activities the borough offers free of charge.
The activities will run from January 1 to December 31, 2026.
The money will be paid in three instalments: $20,000 after the agreement is signed, $10,000 after the mid-point report and $10,000 after the final report.
The money comes from the borough's culture operating budget.
The same amount of $40,000 has been granted to this organization for this program since at least 2018.

The City is awarding a professional services contract (architecture, landscape architecture, engineering) to the group made up of Sid Lee Architecture, Projet Paysage, L2C Experts-Conseils and Ponton Guillot for the new aquatic hub at parc Jarry, in Villeray–Saint-Michel–Parc-Extension.
Total spending of $2,346,056.84 including taxes: $1,675,754.88 for the contract, plus $335,150.98 in contingencies and $335,150.98 in incidental expenses. The spending is covered by the central city.
The project will bring the park's pool and wading pool together in one place, in the north section accessible from rue Jarry, where there is currently a parking lot.

Plans include: a seasonal bathers' pavilion with a mechanical room, a welcome pavilion open year-round, pools for 1000 bathers, a wading pool, a beach, landscaping, a parking lot with 50 to 75 spaces and the City's Wi-Fi.

The City points to the condition of the facilities: a wading pool from 1989 with no change room or toilets and no water circulation, and a pool from 1962 that is cracked, with water loss and insufficient filtration, leading to frequent closures.
Of the 34 people who took out the tender documents, 9 submitted bids; 4 did not reach the passing mark of 70%. The price selected is 46.57% below the City's latest estimate.
The performance of the four firms will be evaluated.
The borough of LaSalle appoints borough councillor Bisma Ansari to represent it on the board of directors of PME MTL Grand Sud-Ouest.
She replaces city councillor Richard Deschamps in this position.
PME MTL Grand Sud-Ouest provides services to entrepreneurs and businesses in the boroughs of Verdun, LaSalle and Le Sud-Ouest.
The appointment was adopted unanimously by the borough council on January 8, 2026 and must be approved by the urban agglomeration council.
No money is attached to this decision.
The borough of Verdun is giving $184,485 to five organizations for six projects, under the Prévention Montréal program.
Action Prévention Verdun receives $27,192 for activities introducing children to reading, writing and mathematics, and $68,333 for mediation and urban safety.
The Table de concertation Enfance-Famille de Verdun receives $39,259 for outreach work with families and young children.
Toujours ensemble inc. receives $25,000 for a community space with workshops, homework help and games for teenagers.
The Maison d'accueil des nouveaux arrivants – Île-des-Sœurs receives $16,666 to train 75 young people aged 13 to 17 as babysitters, for a day camp and for homework help.
The École de cirque de Verdun receives $8,035 for a show created by young people about rights, presented on tour during the summer.
The money comes from the budget of the Service de la diversité et de l'inclusion sociale; six agreements set out the terms of the payments.
The borough of Verdun is paying $12,950 to the Société de développement social to keep two psychosocial workers in place from January 5 to February 6, 2026.

These workers operate in municipal facilities and the areas around them (libraries, sports centres, arenas, pools, parks, the areas near metro stations), working with people experiencing homelessness.
They can refer people to housing, support or follow-up services, and suggest arrangements to help people share these spaces.

The money comes from the unspent balance of the $42,500 received in 2025 from the Service de la diversité et de l'inclusion sociale: $29,550 had been used for the period from September 15 to December 31, 2025.
Since this balance cannot be carried over into 2026, the expense is being taken from the borough's operating surplus.

A steering committee (TRAC, CIUSSS du Centre-Sud, Concertation en développement social de Verdun) meets every six weeks; the organization must submit a final report within one month after the end of the project.
The Ville de Montréal wants to allow Vidéotron to permanently occupy part of parc Victor-P.-Gray, in Pierrefonds-Roxboro, to install a telecommunications tower there.
The planned site is at the back of the park, about 280 metres southeast of the intersection of boulevard Des Sources and 14e Rue.
The installations include a metal monopole about 35 m high, a 6 m² equipment vault, a 204 m² fenced enclosure with a hedge on two sides, a 627 m² access road and an underground electrical supply.
Vidéotron will pay $15,707.09 (taxes included) in the first year, an amount increased by 3% each year on the anniversary date of the by-law.
According to the borough, no existing structure tall enough was available in the area; the project replaces a location first considered on the grounds of the United Church.
The borough notes the visual presence of the equipment at the back of the park, with no conflict with the scheduling of activities.
Construction is planned for spring 2026; final adoption of the by-law by city council is targeted for March 2026.
The City is amending its funding agreement with Les Amis de la montagne and the Centre de la montagne, two organizations active in parc du Mont-Royal.
The addendum adds rules on the protection of personal information, which were absent from the agreement signed in 2023, in order to comply with Law 25.
The organizations collect personal information on the City's behalf and will have to meet the new legal requirements.
The addendum covers the period from September 1, 2025 to April 30, 2026, the agreement's expiry date.
The original agreement provided support of up to $1,181,314 from May 1, 2023 to April 30, 2026.
Planned timeline: directives sent in fall 2025, addendum submitted in February 2026, reporting in spring 2026.
The decision falls to the urban agglomeration council; no communications activities are planned.
The City is adding $52,547.16 (taxes included) to the contract with Peraton International LLC, bringing the total authorized amount from $995,984.18 to $1,048,531.34.
The contract amount in U.S. dollars is not changing: it is the rise in the exchange rate that costs more in Canadian dollars (1.3175 when the contract was awarded in 2023, 1.41 in November 2025).
A reserve is set aside at a rate of 1.5 to cover further fluctuations until the final invoice, expected in January 2026.
The contract is to make the SPVM's computer-aided dispatch (CAD) system, in use since 2004, compatible with next-generation 911; it went live on November 10.
This is an interim solution while waiting for the system to be replaced, planned for the end of 2027.
The expense is covered 100% by the agglomeration, since the SPVM falls under agglomeration jurisdiction, and is financed through a loan by-law.

The City is authorizing the Conseil de l'innovation circulaire (CIC), a pan-Canadian non-profit organization, to submit a funding application to the Green Municipal Fund of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.
The money would pay for a feasibility study on a cooperative container reuse system in Montréal.
The study would look at three sectors: restaurants, food retail and events.
It would map existing suppliers, assess infrastructure needs (washing, tracking, collection), costs and benefits, and recommend a governance model.
The CIC would be the main applicant and the City the main partner; if the funding is granted, the money would go directly to the CIC.
The city council resolution is a requirement of the Fund: without it, the application could be turned down as early as the financial analysis stage.
The summary does not indicate any amount or any expense for the City (financial aspect: "N/A").
City council adopts the 2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Works Program (PDI), which is the list of planned investments in infrastructure and buildings for the next 10 years.
The city council portion provides for $15,830.4M in investments over 10 years, including $1,379.2M in 2026.
For 2026, the investments are divided between $185.1M for the boroughs and $1,194M for corporate services.
The share paid by taxpayers reaches $1,053.7M in 2026 and $13,670.3M for all of 2026-2035.
The total PDI submitted by the City amounts to $25,871M: 67.7% goes to protecting existing assets and 32.3% to development, new facilities and bringing facilities up to standard.
Funding for the PDI comes mainly from borrowing (56.2%), cash payment (27%) and government subsidies (14.1%).
The first three years of the PDI (2026-2028) make up the three-year capital works program required by the Cities and Towns Act.
The urban agglomeration council is adopting its 2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Works Program (PDI), which is the list of planned infrastructure investments over ten years.
This agglomeration portion provides for $10,040.8M in investments over ten years, including $924.5M for the year 2026 alone.
The share paid by taxpayers reaches $785.3M in 2026 and $7,837M for the whole 2026-2035 period.
The first three years (2026-2028) serve as the three-year capital works program under the Cities and Towns Act.
The document accompanies the 2026 operating budget of $7.67B and an overall PDI of $25.9B for the City as a whole.
In the overall $25.9B program, 67.7% of the funds go to maintaining existing assets and 32.3% to development, new facilities and bringing things up to standard.
The urban agglomeration council adopts the STM's 2026 budget, balanced at $1,804,314,410 in both revenues and expenses, which is $27.1M (1.5%) more than the 2025 budget.
The increase comes from $10.5M for indexing goods and services and for collective agreements, and $16.6M for costs tied to investments.

The agglomeration will pay $808.4M toward public transit in 2026, an increase of $45.6M: $39.3M for services provided by the STM, EXO and the REM, and $6.3M for free transit for people 65 and over across the whole territory.
The 2026-2035 capital works program totals $24.1B, including $10.5B already authorized through government programs and $13.6B in projects still being identified or defined.
On the bus side, nearly $2.5B in authorized projects: $1,102.7M to electrify transit centres, $1,078M for 12-metre electric buses and $71.2M in operating technologies.

On the métro side, more than $8.0B authorized: $5,958.4M for the extension of the blue line, $422.9M for its train control system, $829.8M for fixed equipment, $456.7M for infrastructure and $171.9M for station accessibility.

The STM funds itself mainly through debt: its net debt would go from $1.3B at the end of 2025 to $2.4B at the end of 2035. It is aiming for $56.5M in recurring savings in 2026 and is capping the growth of its expenses at 3% per year for 5 years.
City council adopts the City of Montréal's 2026 operating budget: $7.67B, presented as balanced.
The City also tables a 2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Works Program of $25.9B, of which 67.7% is to protect existing assets.
Tax charges under city council's control are going up by 3.4% for both residential and non-residential properties, which the City links to inflation in the metropolitan region.
Adding in borough council decisions, the total increase in property tax charges reaches 3.8% for residential and 3.4% for non-residential properties.
Revenues come 62.7% from taxation, 20.3% from services rendered and other sources, 8.9% from transfers and 8.1% from the shares paid by the reconstituted cities.
The budget is built around eight priorities: finances, homelessness, housing, safety, quality of life and culture, mobility and roads, the East end of Montréal, and climate resilience.
The largest shares of spending go to public safety (17.9%), debt servicing (16.6%), public transit and general administration (10.5% each).
The urban agglomeration council is adopting the 2026 budget forecasts for the operating activities under its responsibility.
The City's 2026 operating budget is balanced and totals $7.67B.
The City is also tabling a 2026-2035 Ten-Year Capital Works Program of $25.9B, of which 67.7% goes to protecting existing assets.

The increase in tax charges under the control of city council is limited to 3.4%, for both residential and non-residential properties; the total increase reaches 3.8% for residential and 3.4% for non-residential when borough decisions are added.
Revenues come 62.7% from taxation, 20.3% from services rendered, 8.9% from transfers and 8.1% from the shares paid by the reconstituted cities.
The budget targets eight priorities: finances, homelessness, housing, safety, quality of life and culture, mobility and roads, the East of Montréal, and climate resilience.
City council adopts the by-law setting all of the City's tax rates for the year 2026.
These taxes and other revenues are expected to bring in $4.8B for the 2026 budget.
2026 general property tax: 0.4631% for the residual category (which includes housing), 1.8524% for serviced vacant land and 1.3893% for unserviced vacant land.

For non-residential buildings, the rate remains lower on the first $900,000 of value (2.0084%) and higher above that (2.5719%). The same approach applies to the tax related to the ARTM and the tax on the debts of the former cities.

The by-law also sets the water and roadway taxes, the tax on advertising structures, the compensations for exempt buildings (including a rate specific to the STM), the interest and penalty rates and the payment dates.
The taxes apply to all of Montréal's territory, calculated on the adjusted value of buildings based on the phasing-in of the new assessment roll adopted in September 2025.
Owners in the former merged cities (Anjou, Lachine, LaSalle, Montréal-Nord, etc.) also pay a tax related to the debts of their former municipality, at a rate specific to each sector.
The City is renewing for 2026 its property tax on the parking lots of non-residential buildings, a tax in place since 2010 to fund public transit.
The rates for sectors A, B and C (the business district, downtown and the southwest area between the river and the canal Lachine) are being indexed by 3.4%.
The rate for sector D, meaning the rest of the city's territory, is going up by $0.25 per square metre.
In sector D, only outdoor parking lots larger than 5,000 m² belonging to 100% non-residential buildings are covered; elsewhere, a 390 m² exemption applies.
The City expects to collect $38.1M from this tax in 2026, under the same payment terms as the general property tax.
The by-law gives the City investigative powers and provides for additional charges or refunds if the tax data changes.
The island's 15 reconstituted cities (Westmount, Dorval, Pointe-Claire, Mont-Royal, etc.) will pay $9,785,916 to the Ville de Montréal in 2026 for downtown expenses.
The amount is indexed by 1.3% based on the Consumer Price Index for the metropolitan region published by the Conference Board of Canada.
Each city pays according to its fiscal potential: Pointe-Claire $1,661,312, Dorval $1,657,122, Mont-Royal $1,165,309, Westmount $1,113,661, and L'Île-Dorval $1,515.
Payment is made in two equal instalments, on March 16, 2026 and June 1, 2026.
The City's usual rules on interest for late payment of taxes apply to this contribution.

This contribution stems from an agreement from March 2016: since 2017, work to develop public spaces downtown has been paid for by Montréal taxpayers only, in exchange for an indexed annual payment of $8M.
The urban agglomeration council is adopting the rules for paying the shares that the related municipalities (the island's reconstituted cities) must pay to Montréal for the year 2026.

Four shares are covered, all calculated based on 2026 fiscal potential: the general share, the water service share, the first responders share, and the one that funds the agglomeration deficit accumulated as of December 31, 2024.
Montréal must send the invoices to the related municipalities no later than January 30, 2026.
Payment is made in two equal instalments, on March 16, 2026 and June 1, 2026.
In the event of a late payment, interest of 1.2433% per month applies, calculated day by day starting from the due date; only the overdue instalment becomes payable.
The by-law does not provide for any financial impact, except for interest where applicable.
The urban agglomeration council is adopting the by-law that sets how much each related municipality pays for its drinking water in 2026.
The provisional rate is $0.3324 per cubic metre of water, applied to each municipality's estimated consumption.
A provisional bill is sent in January 2026, then adjusted based on actual consumption and actual 2026 costs (either an extra amount to pay or a refund).
On top of the supply, treatment and distribution charges, there are general administration fees of 14.55%.
These share payments are expected to bring in $121.7M for the urban agglomeration.
The method of dividing up the costs based on consumption comes from an agreement reached on March 4, 2016 between Montréal and the reconstituted cities.
City council adopts the by-law that sets, for 2026, the water rate charged to owners of non-residential buildings equipped with a water meter, anywhere on the City's territory.
The rates go up by 5% for all consumption brackets compared with the previous year.
The first 1,000 cubic metres used during the year remain free; after that the rate is $0.110/m³ up to 10,000 m³, $0.225/m³ up to 100,000 m³, and $0.690/m³ beyond that.
In a mixed-use building, 225 m³ are deducted per dwelling before calculating the consumption of the non-residential portion.

In buildings held in divided co-ownership, the bill is split according to the ownership shares, unless the co-owners send a different written agreement to the Service des finances before September 1, 2026.
The by-law applies to buildings with a compliant meter as of September 1, 2025, and the City expects to collect $11.1M in revenue from it in 2026.
The urban agglomeration council is setting the shares that the 16 related cities in the agglomeration will have to pay in 2026 to fund shared services.
The general share will bring in $2,898.6M: it pays for things like police, transit, waste materials, social housing, large parks and culture.
Three other shares are added: $221.9M for the water service, $56.1M for the accumulated deficit and $10.3M for first responders.
The agglomeration deficit accumulated as of December 31, 2024 reached $101.5M; since $45.4M has already been collected in 2025, $56.1M remains to be funded.
Montréal pays 81.64574% of the bill and the 15 reconstituted cities share 18.35426%, based on their fiscal potential.
Côte-Saint-Luc does not contribute to the first responder service, since it funds its own.
These amounts will go to the general fund of the Ville de Montréal, and the resolution applies to the 2026 fiscal year.

The urban agglomeration council is updating the by-law used to share "mixed" administrative expenses between the Ville de Montréal and the agglomeration (which includes the island's reconstituted cities).
The list of support administrative units used for the calculation is being updated to reflect internal changes within the city's departments.
Reorganizations within these units moved $1,479,800 in expenses from local jurisdiction to agglomeration jurisdiction.
To cancel out this effect, the 2025 rate is revised to 10.26896% instead of 10.33163%, and 2025 agglomeration expenses go from $2,028.2M to $2,026.8M, for the 2026 calculation only.
The final rate for mixed general administration expenses for 2026 is set at 10.00511%.
According to the Service des finances, the city's organizational structure remains the same as in 2025 and the units involved will continue the same activities.
City council is putting $297.7M from the general fund into a financial reserve used to pay cash for capital works projects under local jurisdiction.
That is $15M more than what had been planned in the 2025 budget.
The money in this reserve must be used for capital expenditures; the Administration says it wants to focus on rehabilitating municipal infrastructure.
This reserve has existed since 2014, and council has allocated money to it almost every year since.
The document specifies that the file is not tied to the Montréal 2030, climate or inclusion commitments, given its financial nature.
The City is putting $175.9M in 2026 into a financial reserve used to pay cash for capital works under the urban agglomeration's responsibility.
The money comes from the general fund, that is, the day-to-day operating budget.
The administration says it wants to focus on rehabilitating and restoring municipal infrastructure.
This reserve has existed since 2014 and receives a payment voted on by the urban agglomeration council almost every year.
The decision falls to the urban agglomeration council, so it affects all the cities on the island for shared responsibilities.
The Montréal urban agglomeration is transferring $385.2M from the general fund into the financial reserve dedicated to the water service for the year 2026.
This amount corresponds to the sums collected from the related cities through the water-related shares: the water service share, the drinking water rate share and the share for the supply of meters.
The shares collected through loan by-laws for drinking water and wastewater work (Fonds Chantiers Canada-Québec, federal excise tax on gasoline) are also paid into the reserve.
Subsidies dedicated to the water service and revenues from the rates required by the urban agglomeration council are also allocated to it.
The reserve is used to fund expenses related to the provision of the water service, without restriction.
The operation has been repeated every year since at least 2014 and is part of the adoption of the 2026 budget.
City council adopts the by-law setting the City's rates for 2026 (local jurisdiction services, not including borough or agglomeration rates).
Generally, 2026 rates are indexed by 1.9%; some increase more because they are rounded up to the dollar or increased by a fixed amount.

At the Complexe sportif Claude-Robillard, several rates and services are being eliminated (annual access card for the multi-sport hall, 5-day trial pass, field lining, bus parking rental); paramunicipal corporations get a 30% discount off the base rate.

At the Stade de soccer de Montréal and the Complexe sportif Marie-Victorin, the City is abolishing existing rates and creating rates for recurring rentals by recognized organizations; an outdoor natural soccer field at Marie-Victorin will cost from $262 to $365 per hour.

At the TAZ, group classes for wheeled sports move to an hourly rate ($25 for ages 17 and under, $27 for an adult), renting a space for a children's party is set at $100, and some discounted admission fees are being removed.

New discounts: 10% for Accès Montréal card holders on admission to the TAZ, 35% on rentals at the TAZ for Montréal organizations working with people with disabilities, 30% for income security recipients living in Montréal at Claude-Robillard and Marie-Victorin.
Admission fees to the Biodôme, the Insectarium, the Jardin botanique and the Planétarium are going up, both at the regular rate and with the Accès Montréal card.
The urban agglomeration council is adopting the 2026 fee schedule for agglomeration services provided by the Ville de Montréal.
The business units reviewed their fees taking into account the costs incurred by the City; some fees are new, others are changed or eliminated.

The fees apply in particular to access to shared facilities: parcs-nature (the beach and the Centre de plein air du Cap-Saint-Jacques, room rentals, parking, camping) and parc du Mont-Royal (the chalet, the pavillon du Lac-aux-Castors).
Non-residents of the agglomeration pay more than residents to rent rooms and sites (for example, a room of 40 to 55 m² for 4 hours: $195 for a resident, $240 for a non-resident).
Rentals of the chalet du Mont-Royal and the pavillon du Lac-aux-Castors are reduced by 25% for public or non-profit organizations that have a place of business in the agglomeration.
The City's official or protocol activities are not subject to these rental fees.
The by-law applies to the 2026 fiscal year and replaces the one adopted for 2025.
The Ville de Montréal will pay out $44,437,500 in total: its 2026 share to the Communauté métropolitaine de Montréal and its contribution to the musée Pointe-à-Callière.
The Communauté métropolitaine de Montréal receives $34,418,000 to fund its operations; this is the portion tied to city council responsibilities.
The musée Pointe-à-Callière, Cité d'archéologie et d'histoire de Montréal, receives $10,019,500 to support its operations.
The amounts are already included in the 2026 budget and will be paid according to the usual terms.
The City goes through the same exercise every year: similar decisions were made for 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.
The document also mentions a mandate to the Commission sur les finances et l'administration to study the 2026 budget and the 2026-2035 capital works program (central city portion).
The Montréal agglomeration is paying its 2026 financial contributions to five organizations and its share to the Communauté métropolitaine de Montréal.

Up to $808,379,200 will go to the Autorité régionale de transport métropolitain for the year 2026, paid upon invoice; this amount funds, among other things, free transit for seniors on the island of Montréal.

The Conseil des arts receives $24,436,700 and the Société du parc Jean-Drapeau $17,039,500, including $15.6M for its operating expenses and $1.4M for the Formula 1 Grand Prix at the circuit Gilles-Villeneuve (agreement valid until 2031).
The Office municipal d'habitation de Montréal receives $550,000 and the Corporation d'habitation Jeanne-Mance $12,000, for social housing and help for homeless people.
The share of $11,807,100 to the CMM covers the scientific facilities component for Montréal.
These expenses are entirely borne by the agglomeration and the funds are already provided for in the 2026 budget.
Montréal is renewing the "Fleuve à vélo" river shuttle agreement with Varennes and Repentigny for the summers of 2026, 2027 and 2028, with an option to extend it in 2029 and 2030.

The shuttle links Varennes, Repentigny and the Pointe-aux-Trembles area (parc Marcel-Léger, Maison Antoine-Beaudry, Route verte), 54 days per season, from the Fête nationale to the last weekend of September.

The borough of Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles will pay $180,982.15 (taxes included) to the Ville de Repentigny for the three seasons, which is its share of the total contract of $542,946.44.
Repentigny is mandated to operate the service; its call for tenders received only one bid, from Croisière Navark inc.
2026 fares per segment, bicycle included: free for children 5 and under, $4 (6-11 years), $7 (12 years and over), $17 for the family fare (2 adults, 2 children), with annual indexing planned.
The amount covers the boat, the crew, the fuel and the schedule signs at the docks; the operator keeps the ticket sales revenue.
The City will pay $15,315,140.15 to the ministère de la Justice du Québec for the salaries of municipal court judges in 2026.
